note: Existing-source, strict-license-screened public gallery. Additional historical photos remain held from this site. Anatomy overlays are teaching annotations, not a separate verified voucher determination.

tiles.heading: 01 · SILKY, MULTIFLORETED REED SPIKELET
tiles.details: The branched plume alone does not confirm species or native lineage. Isolate one ripe ~10–18 mm laterally compressed spikelet; below its florets are TWO persistent glumes, then a lowest sterile or staminate floret and usually ~3–10 fertile florets. The silky hairs belong to the rachilla/callus between florets, not a long awn on every lemma. Archived spikelet panel 3 teaches gross anatomy, not a measured Texas lineage.
tiles.short: LOOK HERE FIRST: one fluffy spikelet contains several florets along a hairy rachilla
tiles.status: ACTUAL SPIKELET PHOTO — SCALE AND TEXAS VOUCHER MISSING

tiles.heading: 02 · THREE PHRAGMITES LINEAGES — TEXAS
tiles.details: Three lineages are important in Texas, not only native vs invasive: (1) P. australis subsp. americanus is North American native; older sheaths loosen/are shed, exposed stems are often smooth and shiny red-brown, and ligules typically ~1.0–1.7 mm. (2) Eurasian P. australis subsp. australis is introduced and frequently invasive; persistent tight sheaths, dull/ridged stems, ligules typically ~0.4–0.9 mm. (3) Gulf Coast subsp. berlandieri occurs in Texas; Kew currently accepts it as NATIVE to Texas, but older USGS accounts describe its historical origin in the southern USA as uncertain/cryptogenic; it may be confused with the introduced form because quantitative characters overlap. Across lineages, compare upper and lower GLUMES from several ripe spikelets and collar measurements from multiple same-population leaves, not just plume color or stand density. Source-labeled Michigan americanus gallery images are native-reference candidates, NOT Hays County vouchers. No existing card photograph is lineage-confirmed by genotype. For a Texas population of management consequence, keep LINEAGE UNRESOLVED until specimen/voucher assessment and, where needed, genetic lineage identification. Peer-reviewed Gulf Coast photo comparison: Kettenring et al. 2012, Fig. 5 contrasts source-labelled berlandieri with introduced Short A, Short B and Delta sublineages, showing why overall reed height/density cannot certify introduced status. Figure is an external study reference, NOT an archived gallery photo or a substitute for genuine sheath/ligule/glume views.
tiles.short: NATIVE americanus vs INTRODUCED Eurasian australis vs GULF COAST berlandieri — do NOT classify from a species-only photo.
tiles.status: THREE LINEAGES DOCUMENTED — LOCAL SUBSPECIES/LINEAGE PHOTO EVIDENCE INCOMPLETE; NO TREATMENT CLASSIFICATION

tiles.heading: 03 · OLD LEAF SHEATHS — RELEASED VS CLINGING
tiles.details: Check several OLD culms in the same season, not tender green spring shoots. Native americanus: senescent sheaths often peel or naturally drop, exposing glossy upper internodes. Introduced Eurasian australis: dry older sheaths often remain tight. Gulf Coast berlandieri: variable and can resemble introduced; a persistent sheath is NOT enough to classify a Texas plant as invasive. Prefer similar-height culms and both naturally attached and loosening sheaths on the same photographed population; record month/date and exact source lineage determination. IMPORTANT SOUTHWESTERN UPDATE (Palmquist et al. 2026): The number of old sheaths retained can change with arid climate and hydrologic regime. Test HOW TIGHTLY mature sheaths clasp the culm, rather than simply counting retained sheath leaves. This Arizona/Utah native-vs-introduced result is not itself a Gulf Coast subspecies test.
tiles.short: Inspect a mature culm: older sheaths loosen on many native americanus plants; usually cling on introduced Eurasian plants.
tiles.status: SOURCE-VOUCHERED introduced COLLAR close-up now present, but older persistent-sheath sequence and matched Gulf sheath photos still needed.

tiles.heading: 04 · EXPOSED CULM SURFACE AND COLOR
tiles.details: On several late-season culms inspect EXPOSED internodes between nodes. Americanus often has red-brown/purple, smooth, glossy exposed stems. Eurasian australis often duller, greener/tan and finely ridged with tight sheaths. Gulf berlandieri may show woody, branching or reddish stems; these features OVERLAP and colors change with age, light and season. Do not label a stand from a single reddish cane. Photograph mature nodes, sheath scars and an upright stand with the same observer/site/voucher recorded.
tiles.short: Look beneath loosened older sheaths: glossy reddish culms support native americanus; dull ridged culms may support introduced Eurasian reed.
tiles.status: PARTIAL REFERENCE PHOTO — source-labelled native exposed stems available; introduced/Gulf matched stems missing

tiles.heading: 05 · TRUE INNER LIGULE — MULTIPLE MEASUREMENTS
tiles.details: Open five to ten mature leaf blade/sheath junctions from several culms and show a 1-mm ruler where practical. Published non-Gulf tendencies: native americanus often has a longer ciliate membrane (~1.0–1.7 mm), introduced Eurasian australis shorter (~0.4–0.9 mm); overlapping observations occur. Gulf berlandieri commonly overlaps introduced forms, so the native-versus-introduced ligule rule is NOT a Gulf Coast ID key. The existing Harry Rose collar photograph identifies WHERE to look but has no lineage-confirmed Texas provenance. A sharp unscaled image still teaches organ placement, but not a reliable measured cutoff. MEASUREMENT PROTOCOL: USDA guidance includes the short ciliate fringe of the membranous ligule in ligule height, but excludes isolated long, easily broken hairs. Select mature leaves from the MIDDLE THIRD of culms; measure at center plus both lateral portions and average. Do not claim a measured native/introduced difference from the white long hairs in the Burke photograph.
tiles.short: Measure the true short membranous ligule and its short hair fringe; don't measure isolated long hairs.
tiles.status: VOUCHER-LINKED INTRODUCED COLLAR PHOTO ADDED — blade/sheath junction clearly shows white hairs; inner ligule membrane NOT measurable; genetically confirmed native/Gulf measured counterparts and matched glumes outstanding.

tiles.heading: 06 · TWO GLUMES — MEASURE MATURE MATCHED SPIKELETS
tiles.details: Remove several ripe attached spikelets from the same vouchered population. For each, photograph the LOWER and UPPER persistent glumes separately at an equal scale. Broad reported lower/upper lengths: americanus approximately 3–6.5 and 5.5–11 mm; introduced Eurasian australis approximately 2.5–5 and 4.5–7.5 mm. These are approximate published diagnostic tendencies, NOT proof from any one glume, and they do not reliably classify Gulf berlandieri. The Harry Rose annotated source images currently show which organs are glumes, but were not assigned to a genetically confirmed lineage; do not back-assign their dimensions. PHOTO TRAP: locate the two persistent basal glumes first; the next longer bract may be the lower sterile-floret lemma, not the upper glume. Do not measure a sterile lemma as a glume and accidentally assign a native lineage.
tiles.short: Separate lower and upper glumes from ripe spikelets; ranges overlap and need population-level replication.
tiles.status: ACTUAL SPECIES-SPIKELET REFERENCE — matched lineage-vouchered dissected glumes with scale missing

tiles.heading: 07 · DECISION AND MANAGEMENT HOLD
tiles.details: STEP 1: Verify Phragmites species via flowering/glume/rachilla anatomy and distinguish Arundo donax or Zizaniopsis miliacea. STEP 2: Consider all three Texas possibilities: native americanus, introduced Eurasian australis, and Gulf berlandieri. STEP 3: Photograph and document the same population's old sheaths, exposed culms, at least 5–10 true ligules and several paired ripe glumes; capture season/locality and collection/voucher where permitted. STEP 4: Check multiple characters together. If traits conflict, if Gulf Coast overlap is plausible, or before a removal decision, seek regional botanist/herbarium advice and molecular haplotype/genetic confirmation when necessary. Species-only pictures never certify a lineage; Kew treats berlandieri native to Texas while some historical treatments considered Gulf origin uncertain. NEW SOUTHWEST RESEARCH (Palmquist et al., 2026): Genetically tested native and introduced reeds from the greater Grand Canyon region showed considerable native morphological variation. Hairy axillary buds and loose sheath clasping helped distinguish them there; a published basal ligule height distinction should not be confused with the total fringed ligule lengths in the older three-way key. This regional result should NOT be transplanted as a diagnostic key for Gulf Coast berlandieri. Never authorize invasive-control action based on one clue.
tiles.short: If several independent traits agree, record a tentative lineage; if Gulf overlap or management consequences remain, leave it LINEAGE UNRESOLVED.
tiles.status: FIELD DECISION KEY READY — local lineage identification scientifically held pending confirmed provenance/genetics

tiles.heading: 08 · RHIZOMES, STEMS AND TRUE COLLAR
tiles.details: Published species-level culms often ~1–6 m, blades ~20–60 cm by 8–32 mm, branched plume ~20–50 cm. Open the true collar: the ciliate membrane is NOT the long white hairs of the spikelet. Existing archived collar panels 2 and 6 are not lineage-confirmed Texas vouchers. Measure 5–10 leaves at 1-mm scale before comparing lineages.
tiles.short: Tall rhizomatous perennial; short fringed membranous ligule inside blade–sheath junction
tiles.status: NEEDS_PUBLIC_PHOTO — REPLICATED TEXAS LIGULES AND ROOTED CULM

tiles.heading: 09 · TWO UNEQUAL PERSISTENT GLUMES
tiles.details: These AusGrass/USDA APHIS values are broad species-level measurements, not a native-versus-introduced cutoff. Lower and upper glume ranges overlap between North American lineages; dissect 3–5 ripe Texas spikelets, separate each glume, label which is lower/upper, and photograph at 10–20× with a millimeter scale. No existing panorama proves these dimensions.
tiles.short: Lower glume commonly ~3–7 mm; upper ~5–9(10) mm, measured on mature spikelets

tiles.heading: 10 · LEMMA, PALEA AND HAIR INSERTION
tiles.details: A fertile lemma is narrow and pointed but lacks a conspicuous true long awn; a sharp lemma tip is NOT itself an awn. Published silky rachilla/callus hairs ~5–14 mm create the plume. Open a ripe spikelet, distinguish the basal sterile-floret lemma, fertile lemma and two-veined palea, and trace hair origins with a 1-mm bar before drawing microscopic arrows.
tiles.short: Fertile lemma ~8–15 mm, palea ~3–4 mm; conspicuous silky hairs grow from callus/rachilla
tiles.status: NEEDS_PUBLIC_PHOTO — 10–20× HAIR INSERTION AND FLORET DISSECTION

tiles.heading: 11 · SEPARATE ARUNDO AND GIANT CUTGRASS
tiles.details: Giant reed (Arundo donax) also has broad canes and a plume, but much of its silky hair is associated with the lemma/floret base rather than Phragmites' long hairy rachilla. Giant cutgrass (Zizaniopsis miliacea) bears separate male and female one-flowered spikelets, not several fertile florets along one silky spikelet axis. Eastern gamagrass has thick sex-divided jointed spikes, not a fine branched plume. Require matched, public-rights spikelet dissections before final ID or management.
tiles.short: Compare WHERE hairs grow and whether spikelets are multifloreted or sex-separated
tiles.status: FIELD COMPARISON — MATCHED REPRODUCTIVE MACROS MISSING

tiles.heading: 12 · GLUME TRAP — DON'T MEASURE THE BASAL STERILE LEMMA
tiles.details: Start at the stalk/pedicel attachment of an intact ripe spikelet. Locate the short LOWER glume and the somewhat longer UPPER glume—the two persistent bracts at the base. The next bract above them can be the conspicuous lemma of a basal sterile or staminate floret, commonly longer (about 8–15 mm) and sometimes mistaken for the upper glume. Never use that lemma length to conclude native americanus. Confirm which bract attaches where, gently separate the glumes from at least five mature spikelets, photograph each with a 1-mm scale and calculate replicated lengths. The current Harry Rose annotated spikelet shows labelled glumes and florets but is SPECIES-LEVEL and cannot prove any one lineage. If uncertain, leave lineage unresolved; Gulf berlandieri can overlap introduced measurements.
tiles.short: Two glumes are at the spikelet base. The next longer bract can be a sterile-floret lemma, NOT an oversized upper glume.
tiles.status: CREW MISIDENTIFICATION TRAP ADDED — EXISTING ANNOTATED ORGAN PHOTO; NO NEW LINEAGE-CERTIFIED GLUME MACROS

steps.title: 1 · Recognize the whole reed
steps.look_for: See the tall, leafy, jointed wetland stems and feathery branching flower heads. This is the whole-plant view to remember.
steps.why_it_matters: A similar tall reed may be Arundo, so use the next two views instead of deciding from height or fluffiness.

steps.title: 2 · Find where a leaf joins the stem
steps.look_for: The broad leaf blade meets a wraparound sheath. At the inner junction is a small, pale, hair-fringed ligule (a little flap). Follow the existing visible arrows.
steps.why_it_matters: The collar confirms part of the grass anatomy, but a hairy ligule alone does NOT determine a native or introduced Phragmites lineage.

steps.title: 3 · Open one tiny part of the plume
steps.look_for: This source-labeled photograph shows a spikelet (a small flowering unit) with two basal glumes and several florets. The silky hairs on the spikelet axis help separate Phragmites from Arundo.
steps.why_it_matters: Use the photographer's existing labels. Do not confuse a long sterile-floret lemma with an upper glume, and do not infer lineage from an unvouchered close-up.

steps.title: 4 · Texas lineage check: don't guess
steps.look_for: This source-identified Gulf Coast Florida photo shows connected stems and outer leaf sheaths. It does NOT show a measured inner ligule or genetically prove the reed is Gulf Coast.
steps.why_it_matters: There are three important regional groups: North American native americanus, introduced Eurasian australis and Gulf Coast berlandieri. Their visible characters overlap. Record 'lineage unknown' when uncertain.

intro: First learn to recognize Phragmites as a species. Then learn its leaf junction and flowers. Only afterward consider whether a Texas stand is native, Gulf Coast, or introduced.
memory_rule: Tall wetland reed → feathery plume → tiny hairy, many-flowered spikelets → lineage needs extra evidence.
safety_note: Recognizing Phragmites australis does NOT mean you've identified an invasive plant. For removal decisions, compare several mature stems, old sheaths, true ligules and glumes; request expert/voucher/genetic help for uncertain Texas populations.
field_rule: Species first; lineage second. Three Texas lineages may look alike. These teaching photographs do NOT establish Hays County lineage or justify control.
photo_data_caution: Missing or restricted comparison photographs have not been replaced by guesses. Source statements are not proof the associated structure is visible in any available photo.
comparison_text: TWO DIFFERENT TASKS: (A) Species identity: Phragmites australis versus Arundo donax and Zizaniopsis miliacea using real spikelets, rachilla/lemma hair placement, and floral architecture. (B) Lineage: subsp. americanus (North American native), Eurasian introduced subsp. australis (often invasive), and Gulf Coast subsp. berlandieri (Kew accepted/native Texas; historical cryptogenic assessments differ). FIRST compare old sheaths and culm surface, THEN repeat true ligule and paired mature glume measurements from multiple culms. Gulf Coast can mimic Eurasian morphology; inconclusive Texas specimens remain LINEAGE UNRESOLVED pending voucher/lineage testing. Photos labelled only Phragmites australis prove species-level organs, NOT subspecies.
